claim: A new study says sniffing chocolate before a workout helps you do more reps.
why: One study using hedged language (might, could) cannot show a reliable effect. Small samples and no replication leave chance and bias open.
strengthen: Independent replications with larger samples, then a systematic review pooling them.

claim: Researchers say a cocoa compound might have anti-ageing properties.
why: The wording is tentative and nothing shows a real-world benefit in people. It is a lead worth testing, not advice.
strengthen: Randomised trials in humans measuring ageing outcomes, then a meta-analysis.

claim: Four papers say wine is unhealthy and five say it is not, so it is probably fine.
why: Counting papers ignores sample size and quality. Five small studies can be outweighed by four large ones.
strengthen: A systematic review that weights studies by size and risk of bias.

claim: A systematic review of many trials found no clear link between paracetamol in pregnancy and autism or ADHD.
why: It pools and appraises all relevant studies, so it is far less affected by any single flawed result.
strengthen: Keep it living: update it as new studies appear.

claim: My neighbour took a herbal shot and her cold vanished in two days.
why: One case cannot separate the remedy from natural recovery or chance.
strengthen: Controlled trials with a comparison group.

claim: A 1945 study said babies should sleep face down, and guidance followed it for decades.
why: Advice built on one study was later reversed when systematic reviews pooled the evidence. The reversal may have cost many lives.
strengthen: Wait for or commission a systematic review before changing public guidance.

claim: A meta-analysis of 20 randomised trials shows the drug lowers blood pressure modestly.
why: Pooling randomised trials gives a precise estimate. Check heterogeneity and publication bias.
strengthen: Confirm with a living review that adds new trials.

claim: A cohort study of 50,000 people links daily coffee to longer life.
why: Large and useful, but it shows association, not cause, because confounders such as lifestyle may explain it.
strengthen: Randomised evidence where feasible, or a review of several cohorts.

claim: An AI tool summarised the research and says the supplement cures anxiety.
why: AI can hallucinate or misstate findings. Without checking the cited sources, the claim has no reliable footing.
strengthen: Verify every cited paper and check for a systematic review.

claim: Many management practices like annual appraisals are standard, so they must work.
why: Popularity is not evidence. Systematic reviews have found weak support for several such practices.
strengthen: Controlled evaluations and reviews of outcomes.
